. That way, any employer could partner up with other local businesses who offer similar products or services. Smaller employers without many similar offerings like healthcare and meal plans could join forces to offer extra benefits.
There is no reason why these kinds of arrangements cannot do well. Several multi-employer plans already exist, and they offer “administered funds,” rather than each employer having to sponsor its own separate account. These plans usually assume responsibility for core management functions, including the creation and upkeep of investment portfolios, as well as ensuring that administrative tasks are performed. Due to some risk involved, existing multiple-employer plans commonly set investment limits between $50 and $500 per employee, while the plan can handle unlimited capital.
There are some minor issues that would have to be addressed, since 401(k) is not the only window dressing. But as Kevin Kelleher discussed earlier this month, if the rules only apply to rightfully established multiple-employer plans, it’s not a big deal. Multiple employer plans could not only benefit members but also other employers in the area, much like the local Chamber of Commerce.
Cheap and accessible investment options are much better than having no access to plans at all. To put it in perspective, the median employer cost per worker is less than $1,000 in a 401(k) plan, according to multiple sources. It’s crucial to note that these rules would prevent the plan’s cost from enabling market manipulation, a problem often exacerbated by loads and fees. Multiple-employer plans can also facilitate greater savings among individuals, thereby ensuring more contributors to Social Security and Medicare, which aids in stabilizing these programs.
Of course, to ensure that everyone is covered by both safety nets, the government has to keep its hands off. It must not create laws or formulate regulations that arbitrarily increase costs or place disadvantages on specific funds, which is precisely what it has done in the past. It’s not to say that neither government officials nor employees have conflicts of interest (the latter being, naturally, quite apparent), but rather that Uncle Sam is sufficiently preoccupied ensuring the current system functions fairly and freely.
